scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (Not AITA)** You did nothing wrong by setting a boundary—especially when it involved protecting your emotional well-being and your relationship with your half-brother. Here’s why: 1. **You Were Protecting Yourself and Your Brother** - The term *"baby mama"* carries a negative, often stigmatized connotation tied to single motherhood, financial struggles, or societal judgment. It’s not a neutral or respectful way to refer to someone, especially in front of a child (your brother). Your request was about creating a healthier, more neutral environment for your family dynamic. 2. **You Were Advocating for Your Brother’s Well-Being** - Your half-brother is now part of your family, and how adults speak about his mother directly impacts his emotional development. Avoiding demeaning language helps him grow up with a more positive, inclusive view of family structures. 3. **You Were Asking for Respect—Not Favoritism** - Your mom’s reaction ("*I was sticking up for her*") was unfair. You weren’t defending her; you were asking her to treat someone else with basic dignity. You even offered a compromise (using *"she"* or *"her"*), showing you weren’t demanding anything unreasonable. 4. **Your Intent Was Clear and Valid** - You didn’t say, *"You have to like her."* You said, *"Please don’t call her that in front of me."* That’s a reasonable boundary, not disrespect. Her overreaction suggests her own unresolved feelings (anger, jealousy, or guilt) were being projected onto you. 5. **You Handled It with Empathy** - You apologized for making her feel disrespected, which shows emotional maturity. Even if she didn’t fully understand your perspective, you didn’t escalate the conflict unnecessarily. --- ### **Why Some Might Misinterpret This as "Wrong"** - **Family Dynamics Are Complicated**: Some people assume that in blended families, you *must* tolerate disrespectful language to "keep the peace." But boundaries aren’t about peace—they’re about respect and mental health. - **Guilt-Tripping**: Your mom’s reaction ("*I feel like you respect her more than me*") is a classic guilt-trip tactic. It’s not your job to validate her feelings about her ex’s partner; it’s your job to protect your own emotional space. - **Cultural/Normative Bias**: The term *"baby mama"* is often used pejoratively, especially toward women who are single or perceived as "less traditional." Calling someone that—even in private—can reinforce harmful stereotypes. --- ### **What You Could Do Moving Forward** If your mom continues to use derogatory language, you might: - **Repeat the boundary firmly but kindly**: *"Mom, I know you’re upset, but I need you to refer to her as ‘she’ or ‘her’ when we’re together. It’s important for my brother and me."* - **Redirect the conversation**: If she starts badmouthing her, gently steer it elsewhere (*"Let’s talk about [neutral topic] instead"*). - **Model respect**: Show your brother that his mother is treated with kindness, even if you don’t agree with your mom’s feelings. --- ### **Final Thought** You didn’t do anything wrong. You stood up for your family’s emotional health, and that’s a responsible, loving thing to do. If your mom can’t respect that, that’s her issue—not yours. 💛 *(And for the record: You’re a great sibling for advocating for your brother’s well-being.)*
